facts.statement: The type species of the genus Elopteryx is Elopteryx nopcsai, named by Charles William Andrews in 1913.
Curator Charles William Andrews named the type species Elopteryx nopcsai in 1913.
facts.quote: In 1913, curator Charles William Andrews named these as the type species Elopteryx nopcsai.

facts.statement: The genus name Elopteryx is derived from the Ancient Greek words for "marsh" and "wing".
facts.quote: The genus name Elopteryx is from Ancient Greek helos (ἕλος), "marsh" + pteryx (πτέρυξ), "wing".

facts.statement: Charles William Andrews originally believed Elopteryx to be a pelecaniform seabird.
facts.quote: The animal was by Andrews believed to be a pelecaniform seabird.

facts.statement: Kálmán Lambrecht named the family Elopterygidae in 1933.
facts.quote: In 1933 Lambrecht named a separate family Elopterygidae.

facts.statement: In 1975, Harrison and Walker removed several specimens from Elopteryx and redescribed them as Bradycneme draculae and Heptasteornis andrewsi to form the family Bradycnemidae, which they described as gigantic two-meter-tall owls.
facts.quote: In 1975, the distal tibiotarsi BMNH A1588 and BMNH A1528, together with BMNH A4359, were by Colin James Oliver Harrison and Cyril Alexander Walker removed from Elopteryx, redescribed as Bradycneme draculae and Heptasteornis andrewsi respectively, and used to establish a supposed family of gigantic two metre tall owls, the Bradycnemidae.

facts.statement: In 1978, Pierce Brodkorb became the first modern scholar to suggest that the bones attributed to Elopteryx belonged to non-avian dinosaurs rather than birds.
facts.quote: In 1978 Brodkorb had changed his opinion after the supposed Elopteryx material was divided among three species in total, and was actually the first scholar in modern times to suggest that these Mesozoic bones were not of birds but of non-avian dinosaurs.

facts.statement: In 1981, Dan Grigorescu and Eugen Kessler proposed that Elopteryx was a non-avian coelurosaurian dinosaur.
facts.quote: In 1981, Dan Grigorescu and Eugen Kessler stated that Elopteryx was a non-avian coelurosaurian dinosaur.

facts.statement: A 2024 study attributed a new femur specimen from Romania to Elopteryx, indicating it was secondarily flightless.
facts.quote: In 2024, a new femur specimen from Romania was attributed to Elopteryx, and the specimen shows that it was secondarily flightless.

facts.statement: Since the 21st century, most studies have classified Elopteryx as a member of the Maniraptora and Paraves.
facts.quote: Since the 21st century, Elopteryx has been supported widely as a member of the Maniraptora, with most studies recovering it as a member of the Paraves.

facts.statement: In 2013, Stephen L. Brusatte and colleagues suggested the possibility that Elopteryx and Balaur bondoc are the same taxon, though they did not consider it the most likely scenario.
facts.quote: In 2013, Stephen L. Brusatte and colleagues mentioned a possibility of Elopteryx and the paravian Balaur bondoc being the same taxon, though the authors did not consider it the most likely case.

facts.statement: In 2024, Stoicescu and colleagues suggested that Elopteryx is a paravian member of Avialae and that Balaur bondoc is likely a junior synonym.
facts.quote: In 2024, Stoicescu and colleagues suggested that Elopteryx is indeed a paravian and a member of the Avialae based on its new specimen, and that Balaur bondoc is probably a junior synonym of Elopteryx.

facts.statement: The Paleobi Database lists the parent group of Elopteryx as Alvarezsauridae.
Elopteryx fossils were found in Late Cretaceous rocks of Romania.
facts.quote: Elopteryx is a genus of paravian theropod dinosaur based on fragmentary fossils found in Late Cretaceous rocks of Romania.

facts.statement: Elopteryx fossils date to the early-late Maastrichtian stage, approximately 70 to 66 million years ago, from the Sânpetru Formation of the Hațeg Island.
facts.quote: The fossils date from the early-late Maastrichtian (Begudian) faunal stage, circa 70-66 million years ago, originating from the Sânpetru Formation of the Hațeg Island.

facts.statement: The time range for Elopteryx is the Maastrichtian stage, from 72.2 to 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Maastrichtian to Maastrichtian (72.2 to 66 million years ago)

facts.statement: In 2019, studies debated Elopteryx's classification, with some recovering it as a basal avialan confuciusornithiform and others suggesting it forms a clade with Gargantuavis and Balaur native to the Late Cretaceous European archipelago.
facts.quote: In 2019, two studies have found it to be an avialan once again, but a basal one; Hartman and colleagues recover it as a confuciusornithiform while Mayr and colleagues note similarities with Gargantuavis and Balaur, suggesting they form a clade native to the Late Cretaceous European archipelago.

facts.statement: Researchers have claimed that the synonymy between Elopteryx and Balaur bondoc remains possible and requires further confirmation.
facts.quote: Mayr and colleagues also claimed that the synonymy of Elopteryx and Balaur remains possible and that more work is needed for confirmation.

rejected.quote: Elopteryx is a genus of paravian theropod dinosaur based on fragmentary fossils found in Late Cretaceous rocks of Romania.

rejected.quote: Initially, Elopteryx was described from its holotype, a proximal left femur, specimen BMNH A1234.
